identity.title: Multi-Domain Riemannian Graph Gluing for Building Graph Foundation Models

problem.claim: How to integrate and transfer knowledge across domains for graph foundation model pre-training.

gap.claim: Existing solutions often do not explain how cross-domain knowledge is integrated or transferred, motivating questions about consistency and transferability between pre-trained and target domains.

contributions.claim: A differential-geometric formulation that merges graph datasets into a unified smooth Riemannian manifold, with neural manifold gluing based on adaptive orthogonal frames.
GraphGlue, a framework for batched pre-training with EMA prototyping and a transferability measure based on geometric consistency.
Reported experiments show superior performance across diverse graph domains and support a geometric scaling law relating more datasets to smoother manifolds and greater transferability.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a fresh differential-geometry perspective and establish neural manifold gluing theoretically for cross-domain graph knowledge integration and transfer.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report superior performance across diverse graph domains in extensive experiments.
The authors report empirical validation of GraphGlue’s geometric scaling law: increasing dataset quantity improves transferability by producing a smoother manifold.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-domain graph pre-training is framed as important for graph foundation models.
Existing approaches are said to leave cross-domain knowledge integration and transfer unexplained.
The paper introduces a unified smooth Riemannian-manifold view and neural manifold gluing via adaptive local frames.
The theory is instantiated in GraphGlue with batched pre-training, EMA prototyping, and geometric-consistency transferability measurement.
Reported experiments indicate strong cross-domain performance and a dataset-scale relationship to manifold smoothness and transferability.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects a theoretical representation of cross-domain structure to concrete framework components and a transferability measure.

lessons.interpretation: A paper can make an abstract integration mechanism more actionable by mapping it to an operational training procedure and measurable diagnostic.
lessons.application: When proposing a cross-domain method, explicitly pair the central structural object with the algorithmic mechanism and a metric intended to reflect transfer.
lessons.exception: This framing may be unsuitable when the structural interpretation cannot be operationalized or the metric lacks a clear relationship to the claimed transfer question.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the graph domains, datasets, baselines, metrics, numerical gains, or experimental conditions behind “superior performance.”
The formulation and assumptions of neural manifold gluing, EMA prototyping, geometric consistency, and the reported scaling law are not detailed.
It is unclear whether the scaling relationship is causal, how broadly it holds, or what dataset quantity and smoothness measurements were used.
